newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - EMU spurred by politics, economics fudged.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - EMU spurred by politics, economics fudged.

text.p: Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) will take place because politicians want it and not necessarily because member states have stuck to the economic rules of the Maastricht Treaty, according to a Reuters survey.
Responses from 34 economists across Europe showed only Luxembourg was likely to meet all five criteria laid down in the treaty setting the rules for EMU.
But this would not stop the march to monetary union given the determination of politicians.

"The closer we get to EMU the more obvious it is that it is going to be a political decision and not a Maastricht criteria decision," said Brian Venables, senior bond strategist at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in the Netherlands.

Rolf Schneider, head of macro research at Dresdner Bank in Germany, agreed: "Political will for monetary union is crucial. It exists and that is one of the reasons why we expect monetary union to happen."
A Reuters monthly poll of 41 European think-tanks and economists showed that, on average, EMU in some form stood an 82 percent chance of getting off the ground on January 1, 1999.

Economists said that although the convergence criteria were important for policy construction, they could not be interpreted too literally or monetary union would never get off the ground. The need for flexibility was apparent in the treaty's wording.

"If you look at the debt to GDP ratio and say, if they don't hit 60 percent they don't make it, then that's not the right interpretation. As long as debt levels are falling they'll be all right," said Nigel Richardson, international economist at Yamaichi in London.
Economists said it was politicians who would decide who should be in and who out, with much of the political clout coming from German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac.

"If Kohl and Chirac were run over at the same time... there would be a real question as to whether the 1999 start date would still be feasible," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist at Bank of America in London.
Chancellor Kohl will be keen to get European unification under way, having already secured his name in history with German unification, some economists said.
Germany's spur to pioneer monetary union is considered idealistic. Already the economic powerhouse of Europe, Germany will strive to be the political powerhouse as well.
French motivation to enter EMU stems from its desire to reduce German dominance within Europe, as well as removing historical, defence-related worries.
Hawkins said French monetary policy was heavily influenced by the Bundesbank. "If we move to some kind of European central bank, that will ultimately dissipate the power of the Bundesbank."
The political stimulus pushing Italy, Spain and Portugal towards currency union was increasing all the time, economists said.
The poll showed that most economists expect Italy to opt for membership of the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) before the end of this year.
But while political momentum from the core and southern fringe countries appears to make monetary union for some inevitable, it is politics which is keeping other countries on the periphery.
Britain is still dithering before a general election expected by May 1997, while Denmark and Sweden must overcome strong internal dissent and constitutional problems if they decide to join.
